chapter_theme: With the Pandya dead on his throne, the fire Kannaki commanded breaks out: the four guardian bhutas of Madurai, each in the form of one order of society, leave the city because its king erred, the fire spares the virtuous, the cows, the children and the elders and burns the rest, the city's housewives judge her revenge no cruelty, all rites cease, and the city goddess, unable to bear the heat, comes before the grieving pathini.

cast.role: the fire god, here called the god under command (ஏவல் தெய்வம்), who burns Madurai at Kannaki's bidding
the guardian gods of Madurai, who close the city's gates
the Pandya king of Madurai, now dead on his throne (named here as செழியன்)
the palace household: the preceptor, astrologer, judges, ministers, accountants, servants and women of the court
the Pandya's elephant-men, horse-masters, charioteers and swordsmen at the palace gate
the first of Madurai's four guardian bhutas, in the form of a Brahmin of the three fires
the royal guardian bhuta of Madurai, in the form of a conquering king
the guardian bhuta of Madurai in a merchant's form, bearing plough and balance
the fourth guardian bhuta of Madurai, bearing the artisans' tools and versed in dance and song
the four guardian bhutas of Madurai together
Kovalan's wife, the pathini whose command has set Madurai burning
the women and men of Madurai
the mistresses of Madurai's great households, keepers of hospitality
the dancing and singing women of Madurai, versed in the sixty-four arts
the guardian goddess of Madurai, who comes before Kannaki

silappathikaram:22:1-15.reading: The fire god under command opens its blazing face and the guardian gods shut the city's gates; not knowing that the Pandya, who gave up his life for the fault of his bent sceptre and so showed the earth a straight one, lies dead on his throne with his queen, the court officials sit still as painted figures, and the elephant-men, horsemen, charioteers and swordsmen crowd in confusion at the palace gate and halt at the sight of the fire.
silappathikaram:22:1-15.nuance: The narrator recasts the king's death as a gift (உயிர் ஆணி கொடுத்து) by which he showed the straight sceptre to the earth (இருநில மடந்தைக்குச் செங்கோல் காட்ட): the death that ends the bent sceptre is itself counted as an act of just rule. The fire is called ஏவல் தெய்வம், the god who takes orders, so the burning is presented as obedience, not as the fire's own wrath. The queen is praised for flawless chastity (புரைதீர் கற்பின்) even as she dies beside the king whose fault brought the fire.
silappathikaram:22:1-15.event: The fire breaks out and the gates are shut while the court, unaware the king is dead, freezes and the guards halt before the flames.

claims.claim: a king who has bent his sceptre restores just rule by giving his life for the fault

silappathikaram:22:1-15.unit_note: End moved from line 10 to line 15: the sentence that begins with the court (lines 7-10) runs on through the painted stillness (11) and the guards at the gate to தாமிடை கொள்ள (15); the description of the first bhuta begins at line 16.

silappathikaram:22:16-36.reading: The first guardian bhuta of Madurai is described in a Brahmin's form: moon-bright with pearl ornaments, crowned with white lotus and arugu, in unbleached cloth and sandal, receiving offerings of honey, milk and sweet smoke at bathing ghats, temples and Veda schools, carrying umbrella, staff, water-pot, kindling and darbha, the thread on his chest, never failing the rule of the three-fire life, with the sacrificial implements of the Veda.
silappathikaram:22:16-36.nuance: The edition marks lines 17-33, almost the whole portrait, as doubted by many commentators; the lines it keeps (16, 34-36) give only the pearl ornament, the unfailing three-fire life and the Vedic sacrificial tools, so no claim is built on the fuller description. The four bhutas that follow are each drawn from one order of society, and this one, the 'first bhuta', is the Brahmin's.
silappathikaram:22:16-36.unit_note: Start moved from line 11 to 16 (the court-and-gate sentence closes at 15); end moved from line 42 to 36, where ஆதிப் பூதத்து அதிபதிக் கடவுளும் closes the first bhuta's portrait; the second begins at 37.

silappathikaram:22:37-61.reading: The royal guardian bhuta is described: bright as the conquering sun, crowned and jewelled, wearing champak and red flowers, saffron on the chest and red silk, receiving hot rice offered in gold, coral-red in body, holding drum, white umbrella, fly-whisk, banner, goad, spear and rope like the ruler of the sea-girt earth, a god like Nediyon who drives off kings, takes their land, wields the straight sceptre, puts down cruel deeds and guards the four lands.
silappathikaram:22:37-61.nuance: Lines 37-50 are doubted in the edition; the kept lines 51-61 carry the whole charter of the royal spirit, ending in செங்கோல் ஓச்சிக் கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து: wielding the straight sceptre and putting down cruel deeds. That is the very office the Pandya claimed when he had Kovalan killed as a thief, so the portrait of the king's own guardian spirit stands as the measure he failed, just before the spirit leaves him.
silappathikaram:22:37-61.unit_note: Start moved from line 43 to 37 (the first bhuta closes at 36); end moved from line 59 to 61, since நானிலம் புரக்கும் (59) runs on through நெடியோன் அன்ன (60) to அரைச பூதத்து அருந்திறற் கடவுளும் (61), which closes the royal bhuta.

silappathikaram:22:62-88.reading: The third guardian bhuta is described in a merchant's form: golden in body, wearing kings' ornaments but no crown, guarding the land by the trading way, holding plough and balance, garlanded with flowers of every landscape, receiving offerings of pulses at threshing floors, fields and market platforms, bringing goods of hill and sea to those who need them, called the master of the faultless life that sustains farming, a great god in the form of the crescent-wearing lord.
silappathikaram:22:62-88.nuance: Lines 67-84 are doubted in the edition, so the kept portrait is short: golden body, kings' ornaments without the crown (64), the trading tradition, plough and balance, and the crescent-crowned form (85-88). The doubted lines garland him with vetchi, thazhai, ambal, neythal, poolai and marutham together, flowers of different landscapes, as if trade gathered every region. Lines 81-82 (தாலு, விலைந்துபத) are obscure and were not resolved.
silappathikaram:22:62-88.unit_note: The core units 60-79 and 80-93 are recut at the bhutas' own closes: this unit starts at line 62, after அரைச பூதத்து அருந்திறற் கடவுளும் (61), and ends at line 88 with விளங்கொளிப் பூத வியன்பெருங் கடவுளும்; line 79 (அவனே) only resumes the subject.

silappathikaram:22:89-106.reading: The fourth bhuta, dark as the karuvilai flower, in dark cloth with flowers of tree, creeper, water and land in his hair, bearing the artisans' tools and versed in dance and song, the chief of the bhutas that receive offerings in Koodal, appears too; and the bhutas say that there is a rule that on the day the king errs in the order of rule this city is to be eaten by fire, and since they know it as their charge, it is not fitting for them to stay.
silappathikaram:22:89-106.nuance: Lines 89-96 are doubted in the edition; the kept portrait (97-102) gives the gem-like body, the dark cloth, dance and song, and the title of chief of Koodal's offering-receiving bhutas. The bhutas' words (103-106) give the burning a law of its own: it is the city's lot (திறன்) when the king errs, and the guardians leave because they know it as their duty (முறை), not because they are driven off. Which order of society the fourth bhuta stands for is not named in the kept lines.
silappathikaram:22:89-106.event: The fourth guardian bhuta appears, and the bhutas declare that the city must burn because its king has erred and that they will leave.

claims.claim: when a king errs in the order of rule, his city is due to be consumed by fire

silappathikaram:22:89-106.unit_note: Start moved from line 94 to 89, where the fourth bhuta's portrait begins (கருவிளை புரையு மேனியன்) after the third closes at 88; the end stays at 106, where the bhutas' words close with எனக்.

silappathikaram:22:107-118.reading: Before the victorious lady who aimed her breast, the four bhutas leave each to its own quarter; the grain street, the chariot streets and the four streets of the separate orders are thrown into turmoil as on the day the monkey-bannered bowman fed the forest to the fire; the flame spares the side of the virtuous and crowds into the quarter of the fighting men, the cows and calves, untouched by fire, reach the broad street of the righteous herdsmen, and the war elephants, cow-elephants and swift horses flee beyond the walls.
silappathikaram:22:107-118.nuance: The fire sorts the city as Kannaki ordered in the previous kaathai: the virtuous (அறவோர்) and the cows are kept from it while the warriors' quarter (மறவோர் சேரி) burns, and the pun அறவோர் / மறவோர் may also mean the righteous against the wicked. விடாது in line 113 is taken as 'not letting the flame loose' on the virtuous, which is how the exemption of 21:53 is fulfilled; read as 'not leaving', it would say the opposite, so the reading is marked uncertain. Line 111, the bowman who burned the forest (the Mahabharata's Arjuna), is doubted in the edition.
silappathikaram:22:107-118.event: The guardian bhutas leave and the fire sweeps the streets of Madurai, sparing the virtuous and the cows while the warriors' quarter burns and the elephants and horses flee.
silappathikaram:22:107-118.unit_note: Start stays at 107; end moved from line 117 to 118, since the sentence on the elephants (117) closes only with புறமதிற் பெயர்ந்தன (118).

silappathikaram:22:119-137.reading: Young women with sandal-smeared breasts and kohl-dark eyes, roused from love-play with their men, stagger in confusion; mothers wake their lisping little sons from cotton beds and go out with the white-haired women; and the mistresses of the great houses, who never failed the household duty of feeding guests, saying with great gladness that the breast-battle of the jewelled lady who lost her husband and won with her anklet is not a cruel thing, worship and praise the god of the blazing fire.
silappathikaram:22:119-137.nuance: The verdict on the burning is given to the wives who keep household dharma (வருவிருந் தோம்பி மனையற முட்டா), and they meet it with great gladness (பெருமகிழ்வு) and worship of the fire: the women of the city it destroys judge Kannaki's act just. The children and elders who leave together are the ones she exempted (மூத்தோர் குழவி, 21:54).
silappathikaram:22:119-137.event: The townspeople flee the fire with their children and elders, and the housewives of Madurai worship the fire god, calling Kannaki's revenge no cruelty.

claims.claim: a wife's fiery vengeance for a husband wrongly killed is not cruelty

silappathikaram:22:119-137.unit_note: Start moved from line 118 to 119 (see the previous unit); end moved from line 133 to 137, since the housewives' sentence (132-133) closes only with தொழுதனர் ஏத்தினர் (137).

silappathikaram:22:138-157.reading: The dancing women of the sixty-four arts, as if robbed of their stage, ask what land and whose daughter is the lone woman who, having lost her husband in this land and city, defeated the king who did not inquire with her anklet and set this city on fire; the evening festival, Vedic chant, fire offering, worship of gods, lighting of house lamps and the beat of drums all cease; and before the heroic pathini, burning with grief for her lost husband, sighing like a smith's bellows and wandering street to street in anguish, Madurapathi, unable to bear the heat of the fire, comes and appears.
silappathikaram:22:138-157.nuance: The ceasing of rites (ஆரண ஓதை, செந்தீ வேட்டல், தெய்வம் பரவல்) shows a burning that stops the city's worship altogether, including the Brahmins' fire offerings that her command spared from harm. The city's own goddess comes because she cannot bear the fire (கொந்தழல் வெம்மைக் கூரெரி பொறாஅள்): a deity is put under the pathini's fire. The dancers' question names Kannaki only as 'one woman' (ஒருமகள்) who won with the anklet, so the city knows the deed before it knows her.
silappathikaram:22:138-157.event: The city's dancers ask who the woman is, all rites in Madurai stop, and the goddess of Madurai appears before the grieving Kannaki.
silappathikaram:22:138-157.unit_note: Start moved from line 134 to 138 (the housewives' sentence closes at 137); the end stays at 157, the close of the akaval.

silappathikaram:22:158-161.reading: The closing venba says that Madurapathi, a lady of victory who holds what Lakshmi, Saraswati and the queen who killed the buffalo demon possess, came before the woman who cut off her young breast.
silappathikaram:22:158-161.nuance: The venba gives the city goddess the powers of three goddesses at once (மாமகள், நாமகள், the slayer of Mahisha), and still has her come to the mortal woman, not the woman to her. கொற்றத்தாள் with தாம்படைத்த is read as the goddess holding the victory the three possess; the syntax allows other readings.
silappathikaram:22:158-161.event: The goddess of Madurai comes before Kannaki.

links.note: In the court the Pandya calls himself the thief and dies; here the narrator says he gave his life for the bent sceptre and so showed the earth a straight one.
links.teaches: The narrator turns the king's self-condemnation into his last act of just rule, so the same death that proves the sceptre bent is counted as straightening it.

links.note: The couplet says the king who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, having failed to examine, dies by his own sentence.
links.teaches: The epic takes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literally, as a king's own verdict on himself, and adds what the couplet does not allow for: that the ruin can be read as redeeming the rule it ends.

gains.a: the unit's claim that the death showed a straight sceptre gains a rule behind it: a non-examining king's fall is self-caused, not an enemy's work
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which self-caused ruin is chosen and becomes the king's one act of justice, which a bare 'he will perish' cannot show

links.note: Kannaki bids the fire god go to the wicked (ஏவ); this kaathai opens by naming the fire as ஏவல் தெய்வம், the god under command.
links.teaches: The title the fire bears here carries over from her command, so the burning of Madurai is presented as a god's obedience to a woman rather than as divine wrath.

links.note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding a crop; the royal bhuta's office is to put down cruel deeds (கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து), and the Pandya killed Kovalan as a thief under that office.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the licence to kill wrongdoers, which the Pandya invoked, being the very office whose guardian spirit now abandons his city, so the Kural's weeding image is shown to depend on the king knowing which are the weeds.

gains.a: the royal bhuta's charter gains a pointed sense: its duty of putting down the cruel is the duty the Pandya misused
gains.b: the couplet gains its failure case, a king who weeded out an innocent and whose own guardian spirit then left

links.note: Tirumular says a land where Brahmins make the oblation dusk and dawn does not decline and its king prospers; here the Brahmin bhuta of the unfailing three-fire life leaves Madurai because its king erred.
links.teaches: Tirumular makes the Brahmins' rites the protection of king and land, while the epic makes the king's justice the condition of the guardian of those rites staying, so the two run the dependence in opposite directions.

gains.a: the Brahmin bhuta's departure gains its weight: it withdraws what the Saiva text holds to be the land's very safeguard
gains.b: the verse gains a limit: in the epic even the guardian of the three fires cannot keep a city whose king has done wrong

links.note: The couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the bhutas say that on the day the king errs in the order of rule the city is eaten by fire.
links.teaches: Both bind nature's order to the king's justice, but the epic replaces the slow withdrawal of rain with an immediate fire on the city and gives the city's own guardian spirits the knowledge of the rule, so the couplet's consequence becomes a sentence carried out the same night.

gains.a: the bhutas' rule gains a recognised doctrine: misrule upsets the order of nature, which the Kural already states
gains.b: the couplet gains a sharper instance where the penalty falls at once on the city as a whole, and the guardians themselves stand aside for it

links.note: The patikam's first moral is that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று); the bhutas name the same fault (கோமுறை பிழைத்த) as the cause of the city's burning.
links.teaches: The patikam promises death to the erring king; this unit extends the penalty from the king to his city and makes it a standing law the guardian spirits obey, which the moral as first stated does not say.

links.note: Kannaki bids the fire spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste wives, elders and children and go to the wicked; here the flame spares the side of the virtuous, the cows and calves escape, and the warriors' quarter burns.
links.teaches: The exemptions she named are carried out street by street, so the fire is shown as a discriminating judgment rather than a blind disaster, and the warriors' quarter is put among those she called the wicked.

links.note: Tirumular says the king whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy goes to endless hell if he fails them; in the burning Madurai the cows and the virtuous are protected not by the king, who is dead, but by the fire itself.
links.teaches: The two list the same protected beings, but the Saiva verse punishes the failing king after death while the epic transfers his duty of protection, in this life, to the wronged wife's fire.

gains.a: the fire's sparing gains a recognised code: these are the beings any king is bound to protect
gains.b: the verse gains a case where the duty survives the king's failure and is fulfilled by another power, which its threat of hell does not consider

links.note: Kannaki says that if she is truly a pathini she will not let the king and Madurai live; the city's housewives, keepers of household dharma, declare her breast-battle no cruelty and worship the fire.
links.teaches: Her conditional oath is answered not by a god but by the wives of the city she burns, so her standing as a pathini is confirmed by the very household virtue she claimed.

links.note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; in burning Madurai the Vedic chant and the fire offering cease.
links.teaches: The couplet's warning that Vedic learning lapses under an unguarding king is shown happening in a single night, and with the cows spared, so the epic keeps one half of the couplet's penalty and lets the other fall.

gains.a: the stopping of the rites gains its doctrinal reading: it is the Kural's named sign of a king who failed to guard
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene in which its two penalties are separated, the cows spared by the pathini's command while the books' recitation still falls silent

links.note: In Puhar's evening the women parted from their lovers sigh like a smith's bellows (ஊதுஉலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனர்); here Kannaki, parted from Kovalan by his death, sighs like the bellows (ஊதுலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனள்) amid a burning city.
links.teaches: The same formula moves from the passing grief of lovers apart for a night to a widow's grief that has set a city alight, so the forge in the image becomes a real fire.

links.note: Madurapathi appears before Kannaki here; in the next kaathai she names herself and tells her that the harm came to her husband as ஊழ்வினை, a deed come to fruit.
links.teaches: The goddess who comes because she cannot bear the fire is the one who will give karma as the cause, so the poem brings in its karmic account only after the pathini's justice has run its course.

links.note: The venba gives Madurapathi the powers of Lakshmi, Saraswati and the slayer of Mahisha; the next kaathai shows her body half dark and half gold, lotus in one hand and sword in the other.
links.teaches: The venba's union of gentle and warlike goddesses is drawn in the next kaathai as a body divided down the middle, so the reader sees the city goddess's double nature first named, then pictured.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 155, வீரபத் தினி)

new_concepts.gloss: a guardian spirit of a city or of one order of its people, receiving offerings and bound to a rule of when to leave

source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 161 lines as shown but the edition's printed last line is 160, so the printed numbering is one short somewhere; the edition's doubted spans (17-33, 37-50, 67-84, 89-96, 111) were applied as given to the lines as shown, and on sense they fit them (each doubted span is a fuller portrait of a bhuta whose kept lines remain).
Line 47 (முகிழ்த்தகைச்) is a single word on a line of its own, probably a broken or split line.
Lines 81-82 (சூழொளித் தாலு மியாழும், விலைந்துபத மிகுந்து) are obscure as written and may be corrupt.
Line 113: விடாது can be read as sparing or as clinging to the virtuous; the sparing reading is taken from the exemptions in 21:53.
